hook: A mineral wall with a battery across it. Warm vent fluid meets acid ocean, and chemistry starts keeping score.
The ribosome arrives: a machine that reads a tape of codons and builds what it reads.
A cell compares now with four seconds ago and swims toward food. Earth's first working memory.
A protein clock ticks once a day. The planning horizon jumps from seconds to 24 hours.
Oxygen poisons the old world and the planet freezes.
Breathing oxygen yields 15–18× more energy from each sugar.
One cell swallows another and keeps it as a power plant.
An eyespot wired to two flagella steers toward light in milliseconds.
Sex turns evolution into a parallel search.
Synapse proteins show up long before any synapse.
Ice from pole to equator for 55 million years. Living biomass falls 86%.
Melting ice washes ground-up rock into the sea. Sponges coordinate pumping across a whole body with chemical waves and no nerves.
Bodies without nerves still coordinate, using peptides and voltage.
Neurons are at work by now. Planet-wide synaptic activity goes from zero to 10²⁰ events per second.
Steering: approach the good, avoid the bad, in three dimensions.
Eyes with 16,000 lenses start an arms race. Neural activity hits 800× its earlier level.
Jet-propelled squid cousins hunt open water while coral clones wire vast reefs. Sea animal families triple and nerve activity jumps sixfold.
Dopamine teaches by surprise. Brains learn from reward.
Ice returns. Most sea species die and neural activity falls 90%.
Life refills the post-ice seas. Early fishes sense water ripples along their flanks and fire split-second escape flips.
Myelin insulates nerves: 50× faster signals for a hundredth of the energy.
Plants spread across the land and start piling up wood, a huge carbon store with almost no living cells.
Runoff from the first forests starves the sea of oxygen. About 75% of marine species die, including giant armored fish, and nerve activity drops 70%.
Eyes leave the water. Visible space grows a millionfold, and planning starts to pay.
Oxygen near 30% powers giant insects over the coal forests.
A waterproof shelled egg frees vertebrates from water, and a three-layered forebrain maps dry inland Pangaea.
Super-volcanoes erupt. Biomass falls 76% and neural activity 94%.
In thin 14%-oxygen air, mammal ancestors grow tactile whiskers and warm nose scrolls while dinosaur cousins evolve one-way lungs.
A two-million-year rainy spell reshapes the land. Fast-running early dinosaurs balance on two legs, and global nerve signaling quadruples.
Warm blood and a layered cortex let small animals hunt at night and replay their routes.
Huge eruptions along the opening Atlantic fill the air with carbon dioxide. About 76% of species die, clearing the stage for giant dinosaurs.
Old jaw bones begin to become a three-bone middle ear for high-pitched hearing.
Flight needs a fast 3D controller, so the brain's balance centers grow.
Petals, scent and nectar turn flying insects into targeted pollen couriers, transforming land ecosystems.
Ant and bee colonies act as superorganisms. Neural activity peaks at 2×10²⁶ events per second.
Impact winter. Neural activity falls 92.5% and the big dinosaurs are gone.
Small warm-blooded survivors inherit an emptied world.
Forward-facing eyes spread through hothouse forests, some mammal brains begin to fold, and global nerve signaling more than doubles.
Whales see with sound; songbirds pack 240 million neurons into each gram of brain.
Deep-diving sperm whales evolve Earth's largest brains and ocean-spanning click dialects while grasslands spread.
Reading minds: a prefrontal cortex that models what others know.
Drying African grasslands reward walking on two legs, freeing hands to carry while elephant and ape families coordinate across kilometers.
A struck stone keeps a plan for 10,000 years at zero watts. Memory leaves the body.
Sharp Oldowan stone flakes butcher meat and marrow, co-evolving with hand-eye brain circuits and multiplying memory outside bodies tenfold.
Possibly tending fire already: cooking digests food outside the body and frees energy for a bigger brain.
Modern-sized brains plan multi-step stone cores and balanced wooden spears, hunting big game in tight cooperative families.
Early Homo sapiens across Africa combine modern-sized skulls, prepared-core stone blades and three-generation family care.
Cross-hatched red ochre and pierced shell beads hold shared meaning outside the skull, multiplying external memory tenfold.
Language at ~39 bits per second, cave art and tally bones.
Domesticated grain and herds turn sunlight into stored surplus, anchoring permanent villages of thousands of people.
Traders seal counting tokens inside hollow clay balls and press their shapes outside: three-dimensional objects become flat signs.
Baked clay keeps records for thousands of years without power.
Shrinking ~800 word-signs down to 22 sound-letters makes reading far easier to learn and spreads literacy along Bronze Age trade routes.
Panini writes ~4,000 exact rules for Sanskrit, Greeks prove geometry step by step, and stamped coins coordinate markets through prices.
Cataloged libraries hold tens of thousands of scrolls or more, bronze gears predict eclipses, and road-linked empires grow toward ~60 million people each.
Bound pages with numbers and tables of contents replace scrolls, letting readers jump straight to any passage instead of unrolling.
Rag-paper mills spread across Eurasia while numbers with a zero turn hard arithmetic into quick, repeatable written algorithms.
Copying cost falls 300× and science becomes shared memory.
Geared calculators add and multiply by turning drums, while the first science journals make discoveries public and checkable.
Signals cross continents two million times faster than a nerve.
Electric pins read holes in paper cards to count 63 million people in the 1890 US census, while radio sends signals without wires.
Computing goes electronic and software becomes data.
Whole circuits etched onto single silicon chips launch Moore's law, paired with electronic DRAM memory and packet-switched ARPANET.
Digital storage nears every paper, film and vinyl archive ever made, and passes it two years later.
Smartphones put networked cameras and maps in a billion pockets while chemists boot the first synthetic bacterial genome.
Graphics chips get repurposed to learn.
One self-attention neural architecture learns to write text and code and predicts the 3D shapes of 200 million biological proteins.
One machine runs 3×10²⁰ operations per second. All silicon together is still 0.006% of animal brain activity, and the typical cell is still a bacterium.
